meta.what: English for each entry of Radak's Sefer HaShorashim the site shows. 'sense' is the line that stands in the root's row, so a reader scanning the list sees what the root means before opening anything. 'more' is what the open panel adds above his Hebrew: a few short labelled parts, each one thing his entry holds. Both are the guide's summary of his entry, not his words and not a translation, and the page says so.
rules: Report only what the entry holds. Where he names a view and its holder, name both. Where he disputes one, say so and say whom. Nothing from outside the entry.
Every Hebrew phrase quoted gets its English, or a reader without Hebrew gets nothing from the part that carries the point.
Lead with what the word means. Grammar is named only where he rests something on it, and then by what it does, since binyan names are not English.
Do not narrate the entry. 'He brings X for reading Y' is about the page; what X reads, and why, is about the word.
A part earns its place by being worth knowing. Where his entry is one line, the gloss is one line.
meta.keyed_by: Radak's headword as references/shorashim.json stores it, so an entry serving two roots (גרז for both גרז and גרזן) is glossed once.

אבד.sense: To be lost, or to perish; and where the verb takes an object, to destroy.

more.t: אֲבֵדָה, a lost object, the thing itself that is lost; אֲבַדּוֹן and אַבְדָן, destruction.

אֲרַמִּי אֹבֵד אָבִי (Devarim 26:5) he reads of Yaakov, not of Lavan: my father was a wandering Arami. Yaakov is the one lost, and he is called an Arami because he lived in Aram, twenty years there in great distress. The proof is Yaakov's own complaint to Lavan, by day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night (Bereishis 31:40).

צון.sense: The small livestock, the sheep and the goats.

more.t: Sometimes it takes in both together (Vayikra 3:6); sometimes one of them alone, as at Shmuel I 25:2, where it is the sheep, the goats being counted beside them; sometimes only the females (Bereishis 30:39); and sometimes the small livestock and the cattle together, as at Shmuel I 8:17, where the parsha names no cattle.
It is a collective and has no plural of its own, which is why the pesukim count with the singular: וּשְׁתֵּי צֹאן, two of the flock, and וְאַרְבַּע צֹאן, four of the flock.
Written with an alef and read as a vav, and it appears as צֹנֶה without the alef.

רמס.sense: To tread down hard and lay waste; and, spelled with a sin, to creep along the ground.

more.t: מִרְמָס, a thing trampled underfoot.

more.h: The word spelled with a sin
more.t: רמשׂ he says is close to it in sense, and the pesukim he brings are of what moves low along the ground: כָּל רֹמֵשׂ בָּאֲדָמָה, every creeping thing on the ground (Devarim 4:18), and הָרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל הָאָרֶץ, that creeps upon the earth (Bereishis 1:28), with the noun רֶמֶשׂ. He glosses them as treading and going.

גרז.sense: To be cut off; the גַּרְזֶן, the axe, is named from it, because it cuts the trees.

more.t: One line, on נִגְרַזְתִּי מִנֶּגֶד עֵינֶיךָ (Tehillim 31:23), I am cut off from before Your eyes.

אחה.sense: אָח, a brother, and אָחוֹת, a sister; and a second sense, אָחוּ, the marsh grass.

more.t: Almost all of the entry is the forms of אָח: אֲחִי in the construct, the plurals אַחִים and אַחְיוֹת, and which vowel the alef takes under each ending. In אָחוֹת, he notes, the vav stands in for the heh of the root.
At the end he gives the second sense, יִשְׂגֶּה אָחוּ בְלִי מָיִם (Iyov 8:11), can the marsh grass grow without water, where the vav again stands for that heh.

ענה.sense: To answer; and by further senses to bear witness, to raise the voice in song, and to afflict, whence עָנִי, the poor man, and עָנָו, the humble.

more.t: Mostly a reply, but sometimes it opens the speech, as וַיַּעַן אִיּוֹב (Iyov 3:2), where Iyov is answering nobody. In the passive, נַעֲנֶה and נַעֲנֵיתִי mean to be entreated, and he says he will return to that under the root עתר.
לֹא תַעֲנֶה בְרֵעֲךָ עֵד שָׁקֶר (Shemos 20:13), do not testify against your fellow as a false witness.
In song, וַתַּעַן לָהֶם מִרְיָם (Shemos 15:21), Miriam sang out to them; and in mourning, for which he brings Chazal's מְעַנּוֹת, the women who keen together, in Moed Katan.

more.h: Affliction, and what comes from it
more.t: וַיְעַנְּךָ וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ (Devarim 8:3), He afflicted you and let you hunger. To this belong עָנִי, the poor man, and לֶחֶם עֹנִי, the bread named for the affliction in Mitzrayim. Close to it he sets עָנָו and עֲנָוָה, lowliness of spirit, and so reads עָנִי וְרֹכֵב עַל חֲמוֹר (Zechariah 9:9), humble and riding on a donkey, with Targum Yonasan.

more.h: A matter one is busy with
more.t: עִנְיָן in Koheles, an affair or occupation. Here he brings his father, Rabbi Yonah and Rav Yitzchak ibn Giat; and he differs from Rabbi Yonah on אֶעֱנֶה אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם (Hoshea 2:23), which he takes in the first sense, of speech.
מַעֲנָה, the line a plowman cuts across the field before turning back.

כבשֹ.sense: כֶּבֶשׂ, a lamb, with כַּבְשָׂה and כִּבְשָׂה for the ewe.

more.t: It is called a כבש while it is within its first year, because one older than a year is called אַיִל, a ram.

כבשׁ.sense: To subdue and to seize by force; also כֶּבֶשׁ, a ramp, and כִּבְשָׁן, a kiln.

more.t: וְכָבְשׁוּ אַבְנֵי קֶלַע (Zechariah 9:15) Rabbi Yonah reads as subduing their enemies with slingstones; Radak sets his own reading beside it, that the slingers themselves are overcome.

כֶּבֶשׁ is a ramp, and he takes it from Chazal in Zevachim: one sloping rise, not steps of stone or wood set one above another. That is why the mizbeach was given a kevesh, steps being forbidden by וְלֹא תַעֲלֶה בְמַעֲלֹת (Shemos 20:23), do not go up on My altar by steps.
כִּבְשָׁן, where stones are burnt for lime or earthenware is fired, as against the תַּנּוּר, in which bread is baked by sticking it to the wall.
כְּלִי חֶרֶשׂ (Vayikra 6:21), an earthen vessel, and יָבֵשׁ כַּחֶרֶשׂ כֹּחִי (Tehillim 22:15), my strength is dried up like a potsherd.

וַיִּקַּח לוֹ חֶרֶשׂ לְהִתְגָּרֵד בּוֹ (Iyov 2:8) he reads plainly: a potsherd to scratch himself with, the Satan having struck him with a dry boil. Others read חֶרֶשׂ as the name of the illness itself, which Iyov is said to have chosen out of all illnesses because scratching it gives some relief. Radak calls that reading far-fetched.

חרשׁ.sense: To be silent and to be deaf, with חֵרֵשׁ for a deaf man; and a second sense, to plow.

more.h: Why silence and deafness are one word
more.t: One who keeps quiet is as though he does not hear what is said, and makes himself deaf.

יַחֲרִישׁ בְּאַהֲבָתוֹ (Tzefaniah 3:17) he reads as Hashem keeping silent, out of love, over sins already done. רוּחַ קָדִים חֲרִישִׁית (Yonah 4:8) he takes as a wind so strong that men are made deaf by it, which is how Targum Yonasan renders it, שְׁתִיקָא.

נטה.sense: To turn aside or incline, and to lean toward someone.

more.t: כִּי יוֹאָב נָטָה אַחֲרֵי אֲדֹנִיָּה, Yoav had leaned after Adoniyah. Rabbi Yonah read אַבְשָׁלוֹם in that pasuk as standing for Shlomo; Radak holds that one man is never named in place of another, and says the same against him on זֶרַע יַעֲקוֹב וְדָוִד (Yirmiyahu 33:26). He brings the Ibn Ezra's reading beside his own.
מִטָּה, a bed, he writes under this root as well as under מטט.

מטט.sense: The root of מִטָּה, a bed; and of נָמוֹטּוּ, to be shaken.

more.h: Which root the word belongs to
more.t: Of בַּל נָמוֹטּוּ פְעָמָי (Tehillim 17:5), my steps have not slipped, he says that in the sefarim where the letter is doubled the word belongs here, and where it is not it belongs to מוט.

וַיֵּשֶׁב עַל הַמִּטָּה (Bereishis 48:2), מִטָּתוֹ שֶׁלִּשְׁלֹמֹה (Shir HaShirim 3:7) and מִטּוֹת זָהָב וָכֶסֶף (Esther 1:6), beds of gold and silver. He adds that they are written under נָטָה as well.
He weighs whether it belongs here too, and ends that it may be from נָטָה, where he has written it.

שֹבע.sense: To be sated and to have one's fill, and not of food alone.

more.t: לֹא תִשְׂבַּע עַיִן לִרְאוֹת (Koheles 1:8), the eye is never filled with seeing; שָׂבְעָה בְרָעוֹת נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 88:4), my soul has had its fill of troubles; כִּי רַב שָׂבַעְנוּ בוּז (Tehillim 123:3), we have had our fill of contempt; and דָּוִיד זָקֵן וְשָׂבַע יָמִים (Divrei HaYamim I 23:1), old and full of days.
שָׂבְעָה and שֹׂבַע, fullness; הַשָּׂבָע, the years of plenty.

בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי (Shoftim 14:15), at Shimshon's feast, he holds is the Shabbos, and the fourth of the days of the feast rather than the seventh of them; שביעי, he says, never means רביעי, since a word is not found standing for its opposite. He brings the other reading as well, that it is the seventh day of the feast, and what follows from it.

דָּוִיד הַשְּׁבִעִי (Divrei HaYamim I 2:15) he holds against Rabbi Yonah likewise: the seventh is not the eighth. Shmuel I 16:10, which counts seven sons passing before Shmuel besides David, he settles by saying Yishai may have had a son from another wife, the brothers from David's own mother being seven with him.
שִׁבְעָתַיִם, seven times over.
